label: Scheduled tasks
summary: Scheduled tasks are a Claude Code feature (March 2026) that lets you set up recurring automated runs using a natural language prompt and a cron expression. Maaike tested the feature by automating a weekly garden health check: scanning for broken links, stale drafts, and tag issues without manual intervention. The feature runs unattended in a sidebar session and produces a report, but cannot chain its output into any follow-up action.
how_maaike_uses: Maaike's angle is practical and sceptical. She ran the health check four times on the same content and found inconsistent results: some issues were caught in some runs and missed in others, and file counts were wrong in two runs. She identifies the core tension as consistency versus serendipity. A coded script would give repeatable, controllable results but would never have noticed the Dutch/English tag mismatch that Claude caught incidentally. A natural language prompt loses consistency but gains that kind of unexpected find. She also flags the open-loop problem: the report lands somewhere, and a human still has to read it and decide what to do. There is no way to connect the output to a follow-up task or automated remediation.
open_questions: What kinds of tasks are actually worth scheduling if you can't chain the output into any follow-up action?
Is the serendipity benefit of natural language prompts worth the inconsistency cost, or does a structured task like health checking call for a coded script instead?
